newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: MobileOne escalates Singapore telecoms pager war.
newsitem.headline: MobileOne escalates Singapore telecoms pager war.

text.p: MobileOne Pte Ltd (M1) escalated Singapore's pager war on Tuesday, slashing prices by 37 percent, undercutting chief rival Singapore Telecommunications Ltd(SingTel).
M1 chief executive Neil Montefiore told a news conference the new prices axed Singapore $5.20 off basic pager services, cutting monthly bills to S$8.80 from S$14.00 for unlimited use.
Montefiore said the package was "clearly looking at new users, price conscious people", but would also be "attractive to those users who are paying about S$10 for basic paging".
The new rate comprises a S$4.80 monthly subscription plus a five cents per page charge capped at S$4 to ensure the maximum charge is S$8.80.
Market analysts said this appeared to be the cheapest of all paging services on offer in Singapore.
"The idea is that we will extend the savings we make on low paging usage direct to the customer," Montefiore said.

SingTel cut its basic paging prices by 35 percent in April, taking its cheapest service down to S$9.50 from S$15.00, a move which undercut the three competitors who entered the pager market on April 1.
Asked whether the move was likely to prompt a response in kind by rivals, Montefiore said: "You'll have to ask them".
M1, formed by Keppel Telecom, Singapore Press Holdings, Cable & Wireless and Hongkong Telecommunications, has won about 5,000 pager subscribers since launching on April 1.
Within 10 days of their service launches, fellow new entrants Hutchison Paging and Sunpage were claiming 15,000 and 24,000 subscribers respectively.
Montefiore said half M1's paging customers could transfer to the new scheme, launched in conjunction with a month-long promotion on its other paging packages.
Montefiore said M1's paging customer base was "in line with our expectations".
The company's cellular phone service has had more favourable response, "way beyond our expectations", Montefiore said.
M1 said it had snatched a 10 percent market share, or 35,000 mobile phone subscribers, within the first three weeks of operation.
